Canon law and civil law citations have been retained in Latin.

div.head: Chapter 29
div.p: § 29. Third part of our second conclusion.

The third part of our conclusion says that the said war or the right to declare it against us has been and is continuous, and will be perpetual until the day of judgment, unless it is interrupted or brought to an end by one of the four means. Let us now see whether it is continuous or whether it has been brought to an end or interrupted. As to the first — namely, that it is continuous — this is plain because the cause of just war against us always subsists. First, because no peace, truce, satisfaction, or petition for remission has ever been discussed: as is known to all who have crossed to those parts; indeed the Spaniards never even deigned to think of it, whether because they always held those peoples in the place of vile and contemptible persons, or because they thought themselves able to attack and subjugate them as if they were Muslims, and accordingly to have obtained them in a just war.

Second, because force and personal injury are inflicted continuously and incessantly upon the living, since they are always held captive in the harshest servitude, and their natural liberty is usurped, and both lords and kings as well as judges and all the people lie always prostrate and subject under it. Whence force or violence is committed each day and continuously, and each day and always is born anew, and is in permanent process and in continuous or enduring act: by which not only is violence continuously inflicted on the subjects, making them obey through fear the tyrants and violent lords — as are individually all the Spaniards who hold a repartimiento or encomienda —, but it is also inflicted on the legitimate natural kings or lords. On those — the subjects — compulsive violence; on these — the kings or lords — expulsive violence: against which war can always be made and resistance offered by right, as we said above. Therefore the cause of declaring war always subsists, and consequently the war or the right to declare it is continuous.

Whence what is necessarily required first in order to interrupt the said right is that the infliction of injuries, lesions, or wrongs should cease, and that the incursion of the tyranny and oppression of the already-mentioned repartimiento or encomienda should cease; because while it persists, or the fear of it being inflicted again, certainly neither peace nor truce nor satisfaction — only remission — would serve to bring the right to an end; and consequently the right and cause of waging war against us, who oppress and tyrannically hold free men, will not cease. And the rule is that pardon for sin is not given unless there is amendment: De Regulis iuris, Peccati, Lib. VI, et 24 q. 2 c. legatur et De Schismaticis, cap. 1, Lib. VI. And so the second is clear, namely, that such war is not declared ended.

As for satisfaction, it is to be understood as the satisfaction that is possible, for as we said above it would be impossible for them to restore with equality what they are bound to restore and satisfy: not only the injuries, harms, and lesions they inflicted on so many peoples, kings, and kingdoms which they utterly destroyed and annihilated — to say nothing of the perdition of innumerable souls whom they sent without faith and without sacraments to eternal torments (for which no satisfaction can be made unless they be assigned to flames far greater than those, if they do not repent) —, but also the immense weights of gold and silver and precious stones and other moveable and immoveable goods: for which not even our kings would suffice to make satisfaction, even if they sold their own kingdoms. Therefore if the Spanish delinquents and offenders were to offer in good faith the satisfaction that is possible, those peoples ought to be content; but what and how great that satisfaction should be is a matter for another time and another consideration.

Finally, the conclusion says: "or by voluntary remission." Namely, because the aggrieved — that is, all those peoples, nations and kings, or their lords — voluntarily and of their own accord, with all fraud ceasing, and all force, fear, coercion, or despair of recovering things, and in a will absolutely free or conditional — that is, conditioned, even by reverential fear —, as in Codex, De his que vi metusve causa, throughout; and in L. 1, §. que onerande, at the end, ff., Quarum rerum actio non datur, and there the Gloss, were to remit the injuries and harms inflicted on them: the Spanish injurers and offenders would be freed, because in whatever manner the creditor has been satisfied to his own will, it is held as paid and satisfied, even if it has not been materially paid, as in Digest., De pignorativa actione, L. si rem alienam et ff., Quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur, L. item liberatura, at the beginning et ff., De accusationibus, L. si rem, § satisfactum.

But at this point it must certainly be noted that there will always be a vehement presumption that those peoples will never of free will remit to the Spaniards what they tyrannically took from them, nor the harms they inflicted on them: both on account of the magnitude of the debts, and still more forcibly because they do nothing now, nor do they do anything, except to avoid some greater evil; and so they always involuntarily have the fear of the Spaniards and of their cruelties rooted deep in their hearts — a fear God has given them. For the fear of the tyrant lasts as long as the tyrant lives: because with the same cause of fear always remaining or enduring, the same effect — fear — must remain; and consequently the oppression and injustice itself endures and remains. This is proved by cap. 1, with what is there noted, De his que vi metusve causa fiunt, where it appears for how long the just fear of the wife lasted: as long as the cruel husband lived. And the Gloss and the Doctors there note that a woman who does something out of fear of her husband is excused and nothing has force in law during the whole lifetime of the husband. And Panormitanus, there in the second notable point, says that fear of death is said to be imminent not only while the sword is being brandished, but also afterwards, if the power of the one threatening is such that death is reasonably feared. And that Baldo, in L. 1, near the end, Codex, De condictione ob turpem causam, says the same holds while the tyrannical statute endures; and Felinus, in cap. significasti, the 2nd, 5th col., number 12, De homicidio, says that for as long as the despoiler is more powerful than the despoiled, violence is said to be done to him. Thus from him. For it is the nature of the human condition to fear one whose judgment now raises up and now casts down, as is said in 16, q. 2, c. Visis. And let this judgment be noted, I pray, if it is fulfilled in those peoples. Whence after fear has been inflicted by some act, that fear is never purged by any subsequent act, not even with an interval of time, while the same cause of fear endures. So says Baldo, in L. 2, Quod metus causa. And these things are very much to be noted in this matter of the Indians, because by them many frivolous objections are peremptorily resolved.

But let us return to the conclusion. Since, therefore, those peoples, together with their natural kings and lords, have against us a most just continuous war or the right to declare it, and no peace or truce has ever been made between them and the Spaniards, nor have the Spaniards made or offered satisfaction, not even minimal, nor even thought of such a work, nor have the aggrieved parties remitted so many injuries and immense and irreparable harms and evils that they have suffered from them; nor has the infliction of injuries and harms and the cruel tyranny itself ceased, but each day and from day to day it has been added to, and they add evil upon evil, worse upon worse: they therefore have the said right or continuous and perpetual war against us the Spaniards; and unless at some point it is brought to an end by one of the four said means, it will certainly endure until the day of judgment. It was said in the conclusion: "as against enemies of the human race," because let the histories be examined from the flood up to today: no nation will be found that has so harmed, diminished, and reduced the human race, and in so many diverse and novel forms of inhuman cruelty, as we have done to those innocent peoples in sixty years.
